item.title: Weekly note: The desk cuts itself if nothing happens
item.description: The stocks desk still reads Risk On at 100% invested, and that is the least informative fact in this memo. Its composite score fell from +0.055 last Friday to -0.205 today, well through the -0.10 line that cuts exposure to half. The model requires three consecutive sessions beyond that line before it acts, and today was the second. The practical consequence is unusual and worth stating plainly: if SPY simply closes flat from here, the desk drops to Balanced at 50% invested on its own. Our scenario check confirms it, reporting a 50% stocks exposure for a price held at today's level over the next five sessions. There is no down-trigger to watch, because the trigger has effectively already been pulled; what we are watching for is a rescue. That rescue is a long way off. The level that would hold the desk at 100% is SPY at $746.32, which is 8.2% above today's $689.81 close. For a model that has been fully invested since April 2025, the asymmetry here is the story: a flat tape cuts exposure, and it takes an 8% rally inside a week to avoid the cut. Should the desk go to Balanced, the flagship's weights change from SPY 35% and QQQ 25% to SPY 17.5% and QQQ 12.5%, with the Bitcoin sleeve staying at 15% and gold at 10%. Invested capital would fall from 85% to 55%, and cash would rise from 15% to 45%. Almost none of this week's deterioration came from the economy. The macro group moved from -0.204 to -0.212 across the five sessions, which is noise. The entire -0.260 decline in the score was price-based: trend, momentum and internals. Taking today's weighted contributions, trend accounts for -0.146, internals -0.113, momentum -0.083 and macro only -0.053. The single largest positive contribution in the whole composite is the calendar group at +0.048, which is seasonality and nothing more. Strip that one favourable factor out and today's raw composite falls from -0.343 to -0.391. An investor should understand that the only meaningful thing holding this call above water is the time of year. The volatility group did something counterintuitive that is worth owning rather than glossing over. It improved, from -0.048 to +0.035, on the day the VIX rose 86% across the week to 35.89. The model treats extreme volatility as a contrarian panic input, so a spike large enough to look like capitulation scores positively. That is a deliberate design choice and it has been profitable historically, but it means the composite is now being flattered by the same fear that is driving prices down. Read the score with that in mind. The shape of the damage matters more than its depth, and the shape argues against a simple reading of broad risk aversion. Equal-weight SPY beat the cap-weighted index by 2.6% this week and by 4.2% over three months. Consumer staples beat SPY by 7.2% this week and by 17.3% over three months. Small caps beat SPY by 1.2%. Semiconductors lagged SPY by 10.2% this week and by 21.4% over three months. This is a concentrated de-rating of the artificial-intelligence complex with real rotation into defensives underneath it, not an indiscriminate liquidation. The honest qualification is that by a different measure breadth is now total: our crash-watch confirmation set reports zero of nine major risk assets above their 200-day average, down 89 percentage points in three months. Everything is below trend; the magnitude is wildly uneven. Here is the observation that cuts hardest against the growth-scare narrative. Gold fell 9.1% this week and silver fell 16.2%, alongside an 8.5% fall in SPY, while the dollar rose 0.4% and the 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5%. In a genuine flight to safety gold rallies. Precious metals falling faster than equities, with the dollar firm and long yields high, is the signature of a rate and liquidity repricing rather than a hunt for shelter. The one place we do see classic risk aversion is credit, where high-yield bonds lost 2.4% against Treasuries this week and 2.5% over three months, enough to put the credit proxy in its worst historical quintile. Credit is the signal to respect here; the metals are telling you something different from what the headlines say. This week's data release cuts against the portfolio precisely because it was good. The University of Michigan's final November consumer sentiment reading was revised up to 51.5 from a 51.0 preliminary print, with year-ahead inflation expectations falling a full point. Consumer sentiment is a stocks desk input, though the source publishes it a month in arrears, so November will not reach the model's macro group until December. The problem is the policy path. Futures put roughly a 95% probability on a Federal Reserve rate increase at the December 9 meeting, and firm data keeps it there. Our macro group sits at -0.212 against a cash gate of -0.25; the three-month bill is up 0.44 points in six months and the 10-year is up 0.81 points, both crash-watch conditions currently on. Strong economic news that keeps the Fed tightening pushes the macro group toward that gate, and it is the gate that decides whether a Balanced call becomes Risk Off at 0% invested. The other desks are on earlier sessions and should be read as such. The Bitcoin desk, dated the November 18 close, is Balanced at 50% with Bitcoin at $63,004; its level to watch is $48,624, a further 22.8% down, which would take it to 0%. The high-beta satellite, dated the November 13 close, is Risk Off at 0% invested. On the crash watch the stocks desk remains at Warning with 6 of 10 conditions on, unchanged on the week, and all 3 of 3 confirmation signals are on. Those confirmation signals carry a caveat we repeat every time: they are candidates from a forward test, selected from 21 tested against 24 warning episodes, which is far more tests than there were events. They are unvalidated and they change no exposure. Ahead of us, Wednesday November 25 brings PCE inflation for October, the second estimate of third-quarter GDP and the Fed's Beige Book, with markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing early Friday. The two releases that actually feed a model input are the November jobs report on December 4, which supplies the unemployment rate, and November CPI on December 10. The Fed decision on December 9 sits between them. As for the flagship itself, its live record stands at -11.08% against -9.38% for the S&P 500 since inception on October 26, across 20 sessions. That is too short to judge, and will remain too short to judge until it has 60 sessions behind it.

item.title: Weekly note: Not a breadth problem: where the damage is
item.description: The obvious story of the week was an AI unwind, and the index numbers support it: QQQ fell 1.2% on Friday and is down 6.6% over the past month while SPY is down 2.3%. But the model's internals say this is not broad risk aversion. Equal-weight stocks are beating the cap-weighted index, with RSP/SPY up 2.6% over three months, and that factor actually improved this week, from a contribution of +0.023 to +0.031. High-yield credit against Treasuries has barely moved, at -0.4% over three months. What has broken is narrow and specific: semiconductors against the S&P are down 16.1% over three months, and consumer discretionary against staples is down 5.7%. The damage sits in the AI complex and the consumer, not in the market's breadth and not yet in credit. The stocks score finished at 0.055, up from 0.029 five sessions ago but down from 0.257 a month ago. Day over day only two groups moved at all: trend took 0.017 off the score as SPY slipped relative to both its 50-day and 200-day averages, and momentum added 0.006 back as the six-month return improved. Everything else was flat. The more useful number is the counterfactual. The single largest positive contributor is SPY standing 3.1% above its 200-day average, worth +0.067 on its own. Strip that one factor out and the score is roughly -0.01. The call is still comfortably above the -0.10 line that cuts exposure, but almost the entire cushion is price being above its long trend, which is the input that disappears fastest in a decline. None of the three desks changed state this week. The stocks desk remains fully invested, 0.155 above the score that would cut it, and there is a second layer behind that: the macro group reads -0.204 against the -0.25 gate it would have to clear for a negative score to mean cash rather than half exposure. So even a break below the line would currently produce 50% invested, not zero. The Bitcoin desk remains half invested, with its score at -0.084 against a -0.15 cut, down from +0.034 five sessions ago. The move there was real: trend flipped from +0.111 to -0.138 as price lost its 20-week average, and momentum fell from -0.243 to -0.412 with the 14-day RSI at 29.8. The high-beta satellite is also half invested on its most recent report, with a relative-strength score of -0.931 and the basket down 15.9% over three months against SPY's 2.3%. October producer prices came in at 0.3% on the month against 0.4% expected, which reads as a friendly print. The model does not read PPI. What it does read, and what the week confirmed, is less friendly. CPI is running at 3.7% year over year, still under the 4% ceiling that keeps the desk's post-selloff re-entry rule available. The three-month Treasury bill is at 4.05% and up 0.44 of a point over six months, which holds the Fed-easing factor at exactly zero. The ten-year is at 5.13% and the 10-year-minus-3-month curve is 1.08 points positive, an un-inversion that scores a full -1.00 and is the heaviest single negative in the macro group at -0.045. Stated plainly: an economy strong enough to keep the Fed tightening is a headwind for this portfolio, and this week made that marginally worse rather than better. Here is the reading that cuts against the week's mood. University of Michigan consumer sentiment at 48.1 is the second-largest positive contributor in the whole model, at +0.025, because it enters as a contrarian input. The worse households say they feel, the more constructive this framework becomes. Anyone treating the collapse in sentiment as another bearish datapoint has the sign backwards here. The same logic runs through the volatility group, where a VIX at 19.3 scores zero rather than negative, because it is neither calm enough to signal complacency nor panicked enough to signal capitulation. The concrete level to watch is SPY at $725.86, which is 3.8% below Friday's close. That is the price the stocks desk's own engine says would move it to half exposure if held for five sessions with every other input unchanged. In flagship weights, crossing it turns SPY 35% and QQQ 25% into 17.5% and 12.5%, leaving the portfolio 55% invested with 45% in Treasury bills. On the other side, Bitcoin would need $87,380, some 22.4% above its last close, to reach full exposure, and there is no Bitcoin downside level inside the grid the engine tested, so its zero-exposure state is not close either. Crash watch is unchanged at 5 of 10 conditions on, status Warning. The newer confirmation set has 2 of its 3 conditions on: only 33% of nine major risk assets are above their 200-day averages, and that share has fallen 33 points in three months. The credit leg is not on. The caveat belongs in the same breath as the number: these are candidate signals on a forward test, selected from far more tests than there were events, fitted against only seven SPY declines of 10% or more since October 2006, unvalidated, and they change no exposure in any desk. The calendar ahead is thin on model inputs and heavy on market events. Retail sales for October land on November 17, the minutes of the October 27-28 Fed meeting on November 18, and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, October PCE inflation and the Beige Book all on November 25. None of those four feed a model input directly. The two that do are further out: the November jobs report on December 4, which carries the unemployment rate, and November CPI on December 10, which carries the inflation reading that governs the re-entry rule discussed above. The flagship's live record stands at -3.18% since inception on October 26 against the S&P 500's -0.95%, across 15 sessions, with a worst drawdown of 5.4% against the index's 5.1%. Fifteen sessions is too short to judge. Everything before October 26 on this site is a backtest, computed with hindsight from rules chosen with that history in view.

item.title: Weekly note: The index held. What sits underneath it did not.
item.description: US stocks had their worst week since early June, driven by a two-day unwind of the AI and semiconductor trade, and neither desk changed its call. The stocks desk is still Risk On at 100% invested, the Bitcoin desk still Balanced at 50%, and the flagship is still 85% invested. That is not the models shrugging. The stocks composite score fell from +0.086 to +0.03 over the week, its weakest reading in months, and the price that would cut equity exposure in half moved up to about $726 from $722. The call did not change; the distance to the next call shrank to roughly 1%. The more useful fact is why the score is still positive at all. Of the +0.03 total, the calendar group contributes +0.048 on its own, from November seasonality and the second year of the presidential cycle. Strip the calendar out and the composite is roughly -0.018. The only group holding the score above water is the one with the smallest weight and the shortest shelf life, and it fades mechanically as November ends. For the call to stay where it is past the turn of the month, something in trend or internals has to improve. Market internals are the single largest drag, at -0.09 of the composite, and their shape matters more than their size. Semiconductors are down 14.3% against the S&P over three months, a reading all but pinned at the model's floor. Consumer discretionary is down 7.3% against staples, high yield is down 1.9% against Treasuries, and emerging markets are down 4.3% against the S&P. But the equal-weight S&P is up 3.1% against the cap-weighted index. Those two facts together do not describe broad risk aversion, which would show up as the average stock lagging the index, not beating it. They describe a concentrated unwind of the market's leadership with a defensive rotation underneath it. The median stock is weathering this better than the index is. Friday's jobs report is the week's most under-appreciated development, because it cuts the opposite way to how it reads. Payrolls rose 165,000 against expectations near 65,000, unemployment fell to 4.1%, and August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000. On an ordinary week that is good news. This week it pushed market-implied odds of a Federal Reserve rate increase at the December meeting to 78% from 70%, and lifted the two-year yield six basis points. Two of the five risk conditions the stocks desk currently flags are rate-driven: the three-month bill is up 0.44 points in six months and the ten-year is up 0.81 points. A strong labour market now feeds the tightening side of the model rather than the growth side. For the next few months, strong data is a headwind for this portfolio's equity sleeve, not a tailwind, and that is an awkward position for a long-only investor to sit in. Fear rose but did not reach an extreme. The VIX closed at 25.6, up about 80% from its three-month low of 14.2, and realized volatility is 19.9% annualized. Even so, the model's volatility capitulation factor still reads zero: by its standard this is elevated stress, not panic, and panic is usually what marks a tradeable low. Consumer sentiment is a separate oddity worth knowing about. At 48.1 it is depressed enough that the model counts it as a contrarian positive, one of the few inputs actively helping the score. Weak sentiment alongside a strong labour market is an unusual pairing, and it is part of why the composite has held up better than the tape. All three of the desk's experimental confirmation signals are on at once: fewer than 60% of major risk assets above their 200-day average, now 33% of nine, a 44-point fall in that share over three months, and high yield against Treasuries in its worst quintile. In the study behind them, that configuration accompanied the seven declines of 10% or more from a running high since 2006. These deserve a heavy caveat and we will keep repeating it: they were chosen from 21 candidates tested against 24 warning episodes, which is far more tests than events, they remain unvalidated on forward data, and they change no exposure whatsoever. Treat them as a flag to watch, not as evidence. The concrete line to know is this. If SPY were to close near $726 and hold there for five sessions with every other input unchanged, the stocks desk would move to Balanced and the flagship would go from 85% invested to roughly 55%, with cash rising from 15% to about 45%. The five-session hold matters: a single bad print does not do it, which is the model's deliberate slowness. Two pieces of options context sit on top of that level. The heaviest SPY put open interest is at the 725 strike, essentially on the model's own trigger, and estimated dealer gamma was negative across the entire range we checked at the Nov 5 close. Negative gamma means hedging flows tend to amplify moves rather than cushion them. None of that changes a call, and dealer positioning is an estimate resting on an assumption that is often wrong. But it is a reason to expect that if that zone is reached, it may be reached quickly. Bitcoin's setup is asymmetric and the constraint is not Bitcoin. The desk sits at 50% invested and needs roughly 11.7%, a move to about $84,800, before it would go fully invested; its score is +0.07 against a +0.20 threshold. The largest single negative input is not price or momentum but the dollar, with the dollar proxy up 3.2% over three months. Bitcoin's route back to a full position runs through the currency more than through its own chart. One nuance cuts against the easy read of Thursday's session, when Bitcoin fell alongside the Nasdaq and looked like levered technology exposure. Over the last 13 weeks its correlation to the S&P 500 is -0.29 while its correlation to gold is +0.54. This quarter it has behaved more like a monetary hedge than a technology proxy, and a single correlated down-day does not overturn that. What is ahead: October CPI on Tuesday Nov 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET, producer prices on Friday Nov 13, and the Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday Dec 9. CPI is the input that matters most here, both because the inflation reading gates one of the desk's re-entry rules and because the December rate debate now turns on it. On our own record, the flagship is down 3.58% since inception against the S&P 500's 3.47%, over ten sessions. Ten sessions is too short to judge, and we will keep saying so until the count passes 60. Nothing here is investment advice, and the model portfolio is hypothetical.
